title: Answering the questions people ask
for: I want to answer my friends' questions
subtitle: Ten questions people really ask about the faith, each with how to listen first, an honest short answer, the longer one, and what a Christian should concede, for conversations that keep going.
intro: This track is for the Christian whose friends ask hard questions over dinner, at work or in a message late at night. Each session takes one real question: whether faith is just upbringing, suffering, science, contradictions, other religions, hell, the church's record, the God of the Old Testament, and goodness without God. The last asks how to keep a conversation going without trying to win it. Every session teaches four things: how to listen first, an honest short answer, where to find the longer one, and what to concede.

It builds on Why we believe it: the reasons, and on the Academy's tracks for the skeptic, which take these questions at length. Here the aim is narrower and harder: to answer a friend, not an audience. A question in conversation is rarely only an argument. It often carries a story, and the story comes first. Peter asked for a reason given with gentleness and respect, and each session ends with a guide for a group where you can practise on one another.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Answering the questions people ask. The group is for Christians who want to answer their friends' questions honestly and kindly. It is a place to practise. Each meeting, someone asks the session's question as a friend would, and someone else tries to answer it, and the group helps both. The leader's task is to keep the practice fair: the question asked as its holders mean it, the answer given without pressure, and every concession the truth requires made out loud.

Each person reads the session and opens its page before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It practises it, using each session's group guide, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, weekly or every other week, for ten meetings, and keep the end time you promised. It helps if the group has finished Why we believe it: the reasons, or is reading it alongside. A leader doesn't need every answer. A leader needs to read the pages ahead, to keep the practice gentle, and to stop anyone from treating a friend's question as an opponent's move.

sections.title: The room
body: Meet somewhere ordinary, a living room or a table at a cafe, and sit in a circle. Have the session's page on a phone or printed. Say at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question or decline to take a part in the practice, that what is said about people's own lives and friends stays in the room, and that no one is being graded.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Fifteen minutes: one person asks the session's question as a friend would, and another answers in under three minutes, listening first, then giving the short answer and one honest concession.
Ten minutes: the group says what helped in the answer and what sounded like winning rather than listening.
Twenty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Let a silence sit before you fill it.
Five minutes: the verse read aloud, and the prayer prompt.
Five minutes: name the next session and the page it opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Some questions in the practice will have no ready answer. Say so, write the question down, and bring it back after reading the longer page. Where faithful Christians disagree, as on the nature of hell or how to read Genesis beside the sciences, set out the views fairly and leave them open. Teach the group to say to a friend what they don't know, and to come back with what they find; that is often the most persuasive thing a Christian can do.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: The practice is play, but the questions are not. Someone in the group may be carrying the question for real: a loss, a parent outside the faith, harm done in a church. When that becomes plain, stop the practice. Listen, thank the person for trusting the group, and don't answer their pain with an argument. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them afterward on their own.

The session on the church's record needs special care. If someone says that anyone is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. Abuse of a child is a crime and a matter for the police, not only for the group.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when a question has become a weight they can't put down: grief over someone who has died, fear of judgment that won't let them rest, harm done to them in a church or at home, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The same is true when a friend they are talking with is in that place. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor.

sessions.title: Isn't faith just upbringing?
teaching: This question often comes from someone who has watched a believer never think about what they were raised with, or who has left a faith of their own. Ask before answering: what makes it seem so to them? Then concede the fact, because it is true. Where and to whom a person is born shapes what they first believe, about God and about almost everything else. John Stuart Mill made the point in 1859, and many Christians hold the faith of their parents without ever having tested it.

The short answer is that how a belief was caused is a different question from whether it is true, and the point cuts both ways, since a skeptic's unbelief also has a time and a place. The longer answer adds that the Christian faith began among people who had to leave the religion of their fathers to hold it, and rests on a public claim, that Jesus rose, which anyone from anywhere can weigh. So the right response to upbringing is to test it, as the Bereans did, who “examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true” (Acts 17:11). Offer to test it together.

open.label: Aren't you only a Christian because of where you were born?
open.why: Mill and Hick on the accident of birth, the fact conceded in full, and why the cause of a belief doesn't settle whether it is true.

also.label: How to answer hard questions about the faith
also.why: Practical help for the moment a friend asks, from listening for the question underneath to admitting what you don't know.

also.label: Is faith just wishful thinking?
also.why: The neighbouring charge, that belief is a comfort people wanted, answered with the same care about causes and reasons.

sessions.question: What did you inherit about faith from your upbringing, and what have you tested for yourself?
sessions.do: Write two sentences you could say to a friend who raises this: one granting what is true in it, and one explaining why the cause of a belief doesn't settle whether it is true.

verse.text: Now the Bereans were more noble-minded than the Thessalonians, for they received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true.

group.open: How much of what you believe about God did you first learn at home?
discuss: Why is it right, and even disarming, to concede the fact behind this question?
How does the same point apply to a skeptic's own views, and how could you say that without scoring a point?
What would it look like to test your faith alongside a friend rather than defend it against them?
group.pray: Those who pray may give thanks for those who first taught them, and ask for the courage to test what they were given.

sessions.title: Why does God allow suffering?
teaching: When this question comes in conversation it is rarely a seminar topic. It may carry a child's illness, a parent's death or a disaster on the news, so listen for which. If it is grief, the first answer is not an argument but presence, and Paul's word to “weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15) comes before any defence. Concede what is true. William Rowe's argument of 1979, from suffering that seems to serve no purpose, hasn't been refuted, and Christians don't claim to know why any particular suffering was permitted.

When the question is ready for an answer, the short one is this: if there is a God of infinite wisdom, we have little reason to expect to see all his purposes, so our not seeing them proves less than it seems. That reply has a cost, and critics press it hard. The longer answer turns from theory to the cross. Christians believe God has not explained suffering from a distance but entered it, and that it will not have the last word. Don't hurry a friend toward that. Sometimes the honest thing to say is that you don't know why, and that you're staying.

open.label: Why does God allow suffering?
open.why: The question faced at length, with the objection at its strongest and an answer that ends at the cross rather than in a theory.

also.label: Doesn't so much pointless suffering make God unlikely?
also.why: Rowe's argument in full, the reply from the limits of human sight, and the cost of that reply, stated plainly.

also.label: Suffering and the silence of God
also.why: For when the question is not an argument at all but a life, yours or a friend's, under weight.

also.label: Find Help: suffering
also.why: Where to turn, or where to point a friend, when the suffering is too heavy to carry alone.

sessions.question: When someone you know is suffering, what is the difference between answering their question and answering them?
sessions.do: Think of someone you know who is suffering now. Instead of preparing an answer, write down one thing you could do this week to stay near them, and then do it.

verse.text: Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.

care: If you are suffering now, your pain is real, and you are not failing God by feeling it. The psalms are full of people who cried out to God. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). Please do not carry it alone: talk to someone you trust, a friend, a pastor, a doctor or a counsellor. If the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. The site's Honest Answer, ‘If God is good, why is there so much suffering?’, faces the larger question.

group.open: What did someone say to you in a hard time that helped, or didn't?
discuss: How can you tell whether a question about suffering is asking for an argument or for company?
Why does it matter to admit that Christians don't know why any particular suffering is permitted?
What does the cross add to the answer that an argument alone can't give?
group.pray: Those who pray may bring before God anyone they know who is suffering, by name, and ask to be a faithful presence before they are a ready answer.

sessions.title: Hasn't science disproved God?
teaching: Listen for which science is meant. Sometimes it is evolution, sometimes the age of the earth, sometimes a sense that every gap where God once stood has been filled. Concede what is true. The church condemned Galileo in 1633 and was wrong to, and some Christians still treat each new finding as a threat. Science has explained a great deal that people once put down to God's direct action, and a God kept only for the gaps will keep shrinking.

The short answer is that science explains how nature works; it can't by itself say whether nature is all there is. The picture of a permanent war between science and faith was drawn largely in the nineteenth century, by John William Draper in 1874 and Andrew Dickson White in 1896, and historians of science have spent decades taking it apart. Many who founded modern science believed they were studying God's works. The longer answer belongs to the arguments from the first track, and to the honest admission that Christians differ over how to read Genesis beside the sciences.

open.label: Does science disprove God?
open.why: The strongest form of the charge, what science can and can't show, and where the real disagreement lies.

also.label: Hasn't religion always been at war with science?
also.why: What the church did to Galileo, said plainly, and how the story of a permanent war was drawn and then taken apart by historians.

also.label: How should a Christian read Genesis 1?
also.why: The readings faithful Christians hold, set out fairly, so that you can tell a friend the church does not speak with one voice here.

sessions.question: What is one thing science can't tell you, and how would you say that without belittling science?
sessions.do: Read Psalm 19:1-4 and Psalm 111:2. Write one sentence a scientist friend might agree with about why studying nature is worth doing.

verse.text: Great are the works of the LORD; they are pondered by all who delight in them.

group.open: Which subject at school made you wonder most about God?
discuss: Why should Christians admit plainly that the church was wrong about Galileo?
What is the difference between explaining how something works and explaining why there is anything at all?
Where do Christians disagree about Genesis and the sciences, and how can those disagreements be held without contempt?
group.pray: Those who pray may give thanks for scientists and their work, and ask for curiosity and humility in speaking about both nature and Scripture.

sessions.title: Isn't the Bible full of contradictions?
teaching: Ask which contradiction they mean. Often the claim is second-hand, and a friend who names one passage is ready for a real conversation. Then concede what is real. The accounts do differ in detail. Matthew and Acts tell the end of Judas differently; the Easter accounts differ on who went to the tomb and how many angels were there; Chronicles and Kings sometimes give different numbers for the same events. Some harmonizations offered for these add what neither text says, and a friend will notice.

The short answer is that differences in detail are what independent witnesses usually leave, and they are not contradictions in what the accounts agree on. Four Easter accounts that matched word for word would look rehearsed. The longer answer takes each case on its own: some are resolved, some are hard, and a few may stay open. Proverbs gives a rule for every reader: “The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him” (Proverbs 18:17). Read the passages together, slowly, and let your friend see you take the difficulty seriously.

open.label: Contradictions: the accounts that disagree
open.why: The census, the two genealogies, Judas, the day of the crucifixion and the numbers in Kings and Chronicles, each faced honestly.

also.label: How did Judas die?
also.why: A worked example: both accounts read side by side, the usual harmonization weighed fairly, and what the two share.

also.label: Do the Easter accounts disagree?
also.why: Who went to the tomb, how many angels, where Jesus appeared, and what the differences say about the witnesses.

also.label: How to read the Gospels
also.why: What kind of writing the Gospels are, which explains why four faithful accounts of one life can differ in order and detail.

sessions.question: Which apparent contradiction in the Bible troubles you most, and have you read the two passages side by side?
sessions.do: Pick one case from the area on contradictions. Read both passages, then write down what the accounts agree on and exactly where they differ.

verse.text: The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him.

group.open: Have you ever heard two honest people tell the same event quite differently?
discuss: Why might it help to ask a friend which contradiction they have in mind?
When is a harmonization fair, and when does it add what neither text says?
How should Christians speak about the cases that remain hard?
group.pray: Those who pray may ask for patience with hard passages, and for honesty that never pretends a difficulty is smaller than it is.

sessions.title: What about other religions?
teaching: This question often has a face behind it: a grandmother of another faith, a kind colleague, a friend from university. Ask who they are thinking of, and listen. Concede what is true. Christians have spoken of other faiths with contempt and ignorance, and the great religions share real goods: prayer, mercy, a moral law that sounds alike in many tongues. When Paul stood in Athens he began with respect: “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious” (Acts 17:22).

The short answer is that Christians confess that whoever is saved is saved by Christ, and that every view of the religions, including the view that all are equal, tells most believers they are wrong about something. So the question isn't who is humble but what is true. The longer answer is that the religions really do differ, above all about Jesus, and that Christians themselves differ over those who never heard, which the creeds leave open. Don't speak for God about a particular person. Speak about what he has shown in Christ, and leave the rest with the Judge of all the earth.

open.label: Is Jesus really the only way to God?
open.why: Hick's pluralism at its strongest, why every view of the religions makes a claim the others deny, and how narrow the Christian claim actually is.

also.label: What about those who never heard?
also.why: The views faithful Christians hold, each in its own terms, so that you can tell a friend honestly where the church agrees and differs.

also.label: Acts 17, passage by passage
also.why: Paul in Athens: what he noticed, what he praised, what he quoted from their own poets, and where he said what they would not accept.

sessions.question: Who comes to mind when someone asks about other religions, and what would you want them to know you respect?
sessions.do: Read Acts 17:16-34. Note what Paul praises, what he quotes from the Athenians' own poets, and where he finally says something they would not accept.

verse.text: Then Paul stood up in the meeting of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious.

group.open: Which friend or neighbour of another faith has taught you something?
discuss: Why does Paul begin in Athens with respect rather than rebuke?
How can you hold that Jesus is the only way without speaking as if you know any one person's end?
What is the difference between saying the religions differ and saying their followers are bad people?
group.pray: Those who pray may pray for friends of other faiths by name, asking for their good and for honest friendship with them.

sessions.title: Why would a loving God send people to hell?
teaching: Listen carefully here, because this question often carries fear or grief: a childhood spent afraid, a parent who died outside the faith. Ask what they were taught, since many people are rejecting a picture the church itself would not defend, a God who enjoys punishing. Concede what is true. The doctrine has been preached cruelly, to frighten children and control adults, and Christians should say so. Concede too that faithful Christians differ on the nature of hell: most have held it to be conscious and unending, while some, John Stott among them, have tentatively held that the lost finally cease to exist.

The short answer is that hell is not God's delight but the end of a life that refuses him, and Scripture says he is “not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). A God who never judged would be indifferent to evil, and the people most wronged in history have not prayed for an indifferent God. The longer answer weighs the views fairly and leaves the second-order questions open. Never use hell as a threat to end a conversation. Speak of it as Jesus did when he wept over Jerusalem, with tears and not with relish.

open.label: Is hell real, and is it fair?
open.why: The moral objection at full strength, the views Christians hold, and why judgment is finally good news for the wronged.

also.label: Is hell forever, or does it end?
also.why: The main Christian views on the nature of hell, each stated as its holders would, with the question left open where the church leaves it open.

also.label: Hell, in the Study Bible
also.why: What Scripture actually says, in its own images, so you can tell a friend what the Bible teaches rather than what they were told.

also.label: How does it end?
also.why: The last things as a whole, judgment and new creation together, and why the hope holds where believers read the details differently.

sessions.question: What picture of hell were you given, and how does it compare with what Scripture actually says?
sessions.do: Write the strongest form of the objection in two sentences, as a friend who holds it would put it. Then write two sentences in reply that you would be willing to say with tears.

verse.text: The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What were you taught about hell as a child, if anything?
discuss: Why is it important to ask what picture of hell a friend is rejecting?
How do the main Christian views of hell differ, and what do they all share?
Why might a God who never judged be worse news for the wronged than a God who does?
group.pray: Those who pray may ask for hearts that grieve as Jesus grieved over Jerusalem, and for gentleness with anyone carrying fear.

sessions.title: Hasn't the church done more harm than good?
teaching: This question may carry a wound: abuse, exclusion, a church that protected the powerful. If it does, stop and listen, and don't defend an institution to someone it harmed. Concede the record, and concede it first. Christians ran crusades and an Inquisition, fought each other across Europe, blessed slavery, and in our own time hid the abuse of children. Christopher Hitchens argued in 2007 that religion poisons everything, and Christians should be the first to grant how much is true in his charge. Judgment, Peter wrote, is to “begin with the family of God” (1 Peter 4:17).

The short answer is that the harm is real and the faith condemns it by its own Scriptures. Cruelty done in Christ's name was a betrayal of Christ, and the same cruelty has been done for nation, revolution and reason. The longer answer sets beside the record what the church also did, such as taking in the infants Rome left exposed. That isn't a ledger to balance. It shows that the poison is older than any creed, which is what Christianity teaches about the human heart, and that the remedy is repentance, not defence.

open.label: Doesn't religion poison everything?
open.why: Hitchens and Paine at full strength, the church's record granted, and why removing religion would not remove the poison.

also.label: How can a faith that ran the Inquisition claim to be good?
also.why: What was done, told plainly, and what Christians should say about it before saying anything else.

also.label: The children Rome threw away
also.why: The other side of the record, the first Christians and the infants their world left to die, told without using it to excuse anything.

also.label: Find Help: church hurt
also.why: For a friend, or for you, when the question about the church's harm is a personal wound and not a debate.

sessions.question: What is one wrong done by the church that you would want to name honestly before anyone else has to?
sessions.do: Choose one episode from the church's record. Write how a person harmed by it might tell the story, then write what the church should say about it, without any defence.

verse.text: For it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God?

care: If you have been harmed by someone in a church, and were told to forgive and say nothing, what happened to you may have been wrong. Please talk with someone you trust outside that situation. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you seen a church do real good, and when real harm?
discuss: Why is it right to concede the church's record before offering any context?
How is setting the good beside the harm different from balancing a ledger?
What would repentance, rather than defence, look like for a church today?
group.pray: Those who pray may pray for anyone harmed by a church, and ask for churches that tell the truth about themselves.

sessions.title: Isn't the Old Testament God violent?
teaching: Ask which passage they mean. It is often the flood, the plagues of Egypt or the command to destroy the Canaanites, and these are hard; they should not be made easy. Concede that they are troubling, that Christians have read them badly, and that the conquest is among the hardest texts in Scripture. Then correct one common mistake gently. The contrast between an angry God of the Old Testament and a loving God of the New was taught by Marcion in the second century, and the church rejected it.

The short answer is that the Old Testament's most repeated description of God begins with mercy, “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger” (Exodus 34:6), and that some of the sharpest words about judgment in the Bible are Jesus' own. These are hard questions about one God, not evidence of two. The longer answer takes each passage in its setting: the language of ancient war, the shape of the whole story, and the readings faithful Christians hold. The contrast between the two Testaments has also fed contempt for Jews and their Scriptures, and a Christian should refuse it plainly.

open.label: Isn't the God of the Old Testament a different God?
open.why: Marcion's two gods, why the church rejected them, and how mercy and judgment run through both Testaments alike.

also.label: Is the God of the Old Testament the God of Jesus?
also.why: A longer essay on the question, for the friend who has read the hard passages and wants more than a slogan.

also.label: Hard passages
also.why: The hardest passages in every book, each linked to the Study Bible's note, so you can read the one your friend names before you answer.

also.label: The violence of the Old Testament
also.why: The ancient world these texts were written in, and how its language of war changes what the passages are saying.

sessions.question: Which Old Testament passage would you most dread being asked about, and what would you need to read to answer honestly?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 34:6-7 and Luke 13:1-5. Write one sentence on what each shows about God's mercy and his judgment held together.

verse.text: Then the LORD passed in front of Moses and called out: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,

group.open: Which Old Testament story troubled you the first time you read it?
discuss: Why did the church reject Marcion's two gods, and why does the idea keep returning?
How does it change the conversation that Jesus speaks some of the hardest words about judgment?
What makes it honest, rather than evasive, to say that some passages remain hard?
group.pray: Those who pray may ask for courage to read the hard passages, and for a refusal of every contempt for the Jewish people and their Scriptures.

sessions.title: Can you be good without God?
teaching: Often the person asking is good and knows it, and suspects Christians think otherwise. Concede at once what is true: you can be good without believing in God. Atheists are not, as a class, worse neighbours, parents or citizens than churchgoers, and Christians who imply otherwise discredit everything true they say next. Unbelievers also have serious accounts of morality, from evolved instinct to Erik Wielenberg's view that moral truths are simply necessary.

The short answer is that the question isn't whether unbelievers can behave well but what makes the word good point at anything real when anyone uses it. If some things are truly wrong for everyone, everywhere, that fits a world made by a good God better than a world of matter alone. The longer answer is the moral argument from the first track, with the Euthyphro dilemma and its classical reply. Micah's summary of what God asks would be recognized by good people of many faiths and none: to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly. The last clause is the conversation worth having.

open.label: Can you be good without God?
open.why: The question taken seriously from the unbeliever's side first, then the deeper question of what makes goodness real.

also.label: Can you be good without God?
also.why: The argued answer, with Darwin, Wielenberg and the Euthyphro set out fairly before any reply.

also.label: Can life mean anything without God?
also.why: The question that often follows close behind, about meaning rather than morals, answered with the same honesty.

also.label: The image of God, in the Study Bible
also.why: Why Christians expect goodness in every person, believer or not: all are made to reflect the God who made them.

sessions.question: How would you tell a friend that they are good without suggesting that they don't need God?
sessions.do: Write down one way an unbelieving friend has been kinder or more honest than you. Then write one sentence on what you think makes their goodness real.

verse.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

group.open: Who is the most good person you know who doesn't believe in God?
discuss: Why does it matter to concede plainly that unbelievers can be good?
What is the difference between asking whether people can be good and asking what makes goodness real?
How might the image of God in every person explain the goodness of people who don't believe?
group.pray: Those who pray may give thanks for the goodness of neighbours who do not share their faith, and ask to learn from them.

sessions.title: Keeping a conversation going, not winning it
teaching: Most conversations about faith are lost by being won. A friend who has been out-argued rarely changes their mind; more often they stop asking. James gave the rule behind every session in this track: be “quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Ask more questions than you answer. Find out what the question carries. Say what you concede before what you claim. Admit when you don't know, offer to find out, and then come back with what you found.

A good conversation ends with the door open, not with a decision. You don't need to cover everything; one honest answer and a question in return often do more than an hour of argument. Paul wrote: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone” (Colossians 4:6). Gracious speech keeps the friendship larger than the disagreement, and salt keeps it honest. And the conversation was never yours to finish. You give a reason for your hope, and you leave the outcome with God.

open.label: How to share your faith without being weird
open.why: Practical help for talking about faith with friends in a way that respects them and keeps the friendship whole.

also.label: Witness without weirdness
also.why: The longer guide to an ordinary, honest witness among neighbours and colleagues, for the whole of life and not one conversation.

also.label: How to have a hard conversation
also.why: For the moment a conversation about faith becomes tense: how to stay honest and kind when the stakes feel high.

also.label: Explaining the faith to others
also.why: The next track on the road, in Explain It: Explaining the faith to others. Take it up when this one has settled.

sessions.question: Who is one person you could have an unhurried conversation with about faith, and what question would you ask them first?
sessions.do: Within the next two weeks, ask one friend what they think about God, or about one of this track's questions. Listen for most of the time, and end by asking whether you can talk again.

verse.text: Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.

group.open: What is the best conversation about faith you have ever had, and what made it good?
discuss: Why do won arguments so often end conversations?
Which of this track's questions would you now feel most ready to talk about, and which least?
What would it mean to trust the outcome of a conversation to God?
group.pray: Those who pray may name before God the friends they hope to talk with, and ask for patience, honesty and gentleness.
